title: Race, Priesthood, and Temple Blessings
introduction: Remembering Black Latter-day Saints, studying the historical restrictions, and receiving the 1978 revelation with reverence.

sections.title: The historical restrictions and the limits of the record
paragraphs: The Church’s Gospel Topics essay describes a few Black men receiving priesthood ordination during Joseph Smith’s lifetime. In 1852, Brigham Young publicly announced a restriction on ordaining men of Black African descent. Over subsequent decades, Black women and men were also restricted from receiving temple endowment and sealing ordinances. Black people continued to join the Church through baptism and confirmation. These distinctions matter when reading the lives of individual members.

The Church’s current Topics and Questions article states that there is no documented revelation establishing the restriction’s origin. It explains that later Church Presidents believed revelation was needed to end it. The article counsels against speculation. We can acknowledge what the records establish without assigning causes or motives beyond what those sources document. The Church disavows past racial explanations for the restriction.

sections.title: Elijah Able: a life of faith and service
paragraphs: Elijah Able joined the Church in 1832. In 1836, Ambrose Palmer ordained him to the Melchizedek Priesthood; later that year he was ordained a Seventy. A carpenter and missionary, Elijah served in New York and Canada and later helped build the Salt Lake Temple. He and his wife, Mary Ann Adams, raised a family. His history is part of the story of the Saints who worked, worshipped, and shared their faith in the early Church.

Elijah retained his priesthood office after the restriction was announced. Yet his requests to receive his endowment and be sealed to Mary Ann were denied, including another request in 1879. His earlier participation in washing and anointing in Kirtland was distinct from the later temple endowment he sought. The Church’s biography records both his continued service and these unfulfilled requests. He remained faithful until his death in 1884.

sections.title: Jane Manning James: devotion and a desire for temple blessings
paragraphs: Jane Elizabeth Manning James joined the Church in the winter of 1842–43 and reached Utah in 1847. She contributed to temple construction, participated in Relief Society, and provided for her family. Between 1884 and 1904, she repeatedly asked Church leaders for her endowment and sealing blessings. In 1888, she received permission to perform baptisms for deceased relatives. Her requests reveal how deeply temple worship mattered to her.

Jane did not receive her endowment or family sealings during her lifetime. The Church’s biography also describes an unusual 1894 proxy sealing to Joseph Smith’s household as a servant; this did not fulfill her requests for endowment and family sealing. She died in 1908, and those ordinances were performed on her behalf in 1979. Her faith and her efforts to receive temple blessings should be remembered together, with care for the person whose life the records preserve.

sections.title: Families and believers across nations
paragraphs: In Brazil, Helvécio and Rudá Martins welcomed missionaries in 1972 and joined the Church. Helvécio later served on the São Paulo Temple public relations committee while expecting that the restriction would prevent him from receiving its ordinances. The Church’s account, “Joy of an Eternal Covenant,” remembers the couple’s gratitude when they learned of the revelation. They were subsequently sealed in the São Paulo Temple. Read their account as the story of a family seeking the Lord and cherishing His covenants.

In Ghana, Joseph William Billy Johnson, Raphael Abraham Frank Mensah, Rebecca Mould, and other believers shared the Book of Mormon and gathered for worship before the Church was officially established there. These were congregations of believers awaiting baptism and formal organization. The Church’s Ghana history recounts Johnson hearing news of the revelation on the radio in the summer of 1978. On December 9, Johnson, Mensah, and 123 other converts were baptized; a branch was organized in Cape Coast the next morning.

sections.title: The 1978 revelation: prayer and sacred confirmation
paragraphs: President Spencer W. Kimball sought the Lord’s will through prayer, study, and counsel with other Church leaders. “Witnessing the Faithfulness,” in Revelations in Context, places that seeking alongside the lives of Black members and believers. By early 1978, President Kimball was spending many hours praying in the temple. His counselors and the Apostles were also studying and praying about extending priesthood and temple blessings.

Official Declaration 2 records that the revelation was affirmed to Church leaders in the Salt Lake Temple on June 1, 1978. The First Presidency’s letter, dated June 8, announced that every worthy male Church member could be ordained without regard to race or color, and that members and their loved ones could receive temple blessings. On September 30, N. Eldon Tanner presented the revelation in general conference. The assembly unanimously sustained it. These are distinct moments: sacred confirmation, the written announcement, and the Church’s public acceptance.

sources.label: Witnessing the Faithfulness · Revelations in Context

sections.title: Equal worth, temple blessings, and our care for one another
paragraphs: The revelation opened the way for Black men to receive priesthood ordination and for Black women and men to receive temple endowment and sealing ordinances. The Gospel Topics essay describes members responding with joy and entering temples throughout the world. Its concluding teaching affirms that redemption through Jesus Christ is available to the whole human family. Race does not determine a person’s standing before God.

The Church today rejects theories that associate Black skin with divine disfavor or conduct before birth, condemn interracial marriage, or claim that one race is inferior to another. Its current teaching calls members to repent of racial prejudice and oppose racism. Studying this history invites us to listen carefully, speak truthfully, and treat one another with the dignity and love owed to every child of God.

parent_introduction: Priesthood and temple blessings are sacred to Latter-day Saints. This history also touches the lives of Black women, men, and families who sought those blessings while racial restrictions were in place. Their faith, service, and experiences deserve thoughtful attention.
parent_continuation: Continue with a dedicated study of the Church’s historical accounts, the 1978 revelation, and its teachings about the equal worth of every child of God. Read the sources, remember the people, and take time with your questions.
